Female Yellowtail flounder from the Grand Bank attain a maximum total length of 64 cm [Li = 64 cm], a size that places them among the larger pleuronectids in the northwestern Atlantic. A gravid individual measuring 51 cm produces approximately 2,020 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2,020 eggs per spawning event] when water temperatures reach 7 °C [T = 7 °C], with multiple spawning events contributing to the species' high reproductive output. The onset of vitellogenesis and the capacity to spawn repeatedly across the season underscore the species' high reproductive investment. The length at which females first achieve puberty is 29.9 cm [Lp = 29.9 cm], a value that corresponds roughly to ages of 2 to 3 years depending on local thermal history and prey availability. This size-based threshold for reproductive activation ensures that individuals allocate resources to somatic growth before committing to gamete production, a strategy common among iteroparous flatfishes.

Eggs of Yellowtail flounder are demersal and adhesive, with each fertilised ovum containing a yolk supply sufficient to sustain the embryo through the cleavage and blastula stages until eclosion. The wet weight at birth of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is 0.00035 grams [Wwb = 0.00035 grams], a mass derived from the egg diameter of 0.88 mm and representing the lecithotrophic phase before exogenous feeding begins. Larvae remain endotrophic for several days post-hatching, relying on progressively absorbed yolk nutrients while their mouth gapes develop and retinal differentiation advances. The small initial mass places hatchlings in the lower range of values reported for related flatfish species such as Limanda limanda. Once first exogenous feeding commences, larvae must encounter suitable planktonic prey within a critical window, as the depletion of endogenous yolk reserves imposes a narrow margin for successful trophic transition and survival.

The ultimate wet weight an adult female can achieve is 1,500 grams [Wwi = 1,500 grams], a substantial body mass that is attained only after several years of sustained growth on the productive feeding grounds of the Grand Bank. This asymptotic mass is consistent with the maximum recorded total length of 64 cm and reflects the energetic demands of a demersal piscivorous and polychaete-based diet. Available data from trawl surveys indicate that individuals rarely exceed this mass, with most reproductively active females weighing between 800 and 1,200 grams. The attainment of ultimate wet weight coincides with the plateau in somatic growth observed in older age classes, a pattern typical of determinate or near-determinate growth in temperate marine teleosts. Body condition indices suggest that females channel surplus energy into gonad recrudescence rather than continued somatic expansion once this mass is reached.

Longevity in Yellowtail flounder has been estimated from otolith annuli and mark-recapture studies conducted at a mean annual water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], yielding a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years]. This value is comparable to that of other commercially exploited flatfishes in the region, such as American plaice, but shorter than the lifespans reported for deeper-dwelling pleuronectids. The age structure of the Grand Bank population indicates that the majority of individuals die before reaching this maximum, owing to natural mortality from predation and the selective pressure of trawl fisheries. The time since birth at which female puberty occurs, at a water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], is 1,935 days since birth [tp = 1,935 days since birth], meaning that most females do not begin vitellogenesis until their sixth year of life. This delayed reproductive maturity, combined with a moderate maximum lifespan, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises adult survival and repeated spawning opportunities over early reproduction.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the Grand Bank, where bottom water temperatures average 7 °C [T = 7 °C], female Yellowtail flounder at 51 cm produce about 2,020 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = about 2,020 eggs per spawning event], and spawn multiple times per season [F_R_i = multiple times per season], leading to an annual fecundity potentially exceeding 700,000 eggs when the protracted spawning season of several months is considered. Field observations from the Grand Bank dataset confirm that spawning activity peaks during late spring and early summer, with individual females releasing multiple batches of pelagic eggs over the course of several weeks. The daily egg production rate corresponding to these values reflects an optimised balance between fecundity and egg size, given the small wet weight at birth of the resulting larvae. Comparative data from other populations suggest that this reproductive output is sensitive to local food availability and thermal regime, with lower temperatures generally prolonging the interval between spawning events.
